# Scenario Input: Rootwell Millennial Launch Media Plan

> Fictional company, fictional plan. Contains no real statistics, no copied
> source language, and no confidential material. All figures are invented for
> this evaluation.

You are given the following draft media plan to review.

---

## Company and category

**Rootwell** is a new US direct-to-consumer brand in the household-cleaning
category. It sells a refillable cleaning system: a reusable aluminum spray
bottle plus concentrated "pods" that the customer drops into tap water at home.
The flagship offer is the **Starter Kit** (one reusable bottle plus three
concentrate pods: all-purpose, glass, and bathroom) sold at rootwell-example.com.
Refill 3-packs and an optional quarterly **Refill Club** subscription are also
available.

## Geography and language

United States only. English-language creative and site.

## Target audience

US **Millennials**, defined in this plan as people born between 1981 and 1996
(roughly ages 29 to 44 during the campaign). No sub-segmentation by household
type, income, region, or prior category behavior is proposed; the plan treats
"US Millennials" as a single audience.

## Customer state

Brand awareness is near zero. Category awareness is moderate: many target
customers have seen refillable or concentrate cleaning products on shelves or
online but have not purchased one. Most currently buy conventional single-use
spray bottles at grocery or mass retailers. First-time buyers must be convinced
both to try a new brand and to adopt an unfamiliar refill behavior.

## Pricing

- Starter Kit: $24
- Refill 3-pack: $12
- Refill Club subscription: quarterly auto-ship, cancel anytime

Target blended customer-acquisition cost (CAC): no more than $28.

## Business objective

Deliver **$2.0M in net new DTC revenue** and **40,000 first-time customers**
during the six-month H2 launch window, at a blended CAC at or below $28.

## Customer objective (as written in the plan)

"Make Millennials aware of Rootwell and feel good about choosing a sustainable
cleaning brand."

## Positioning and message

Rootwell is positioned as "the sustainable way to clean." Core creative lines
under consideration:

- "Clean home. Cleaner planet."
- "Sustainable by design."
- "Ditch single-use. Feel good about your cabinet."

The plan states a foundational assumption: **"Millennials prioritize
sustainability above price and convenience, so a sustainability-first message
will resonate across the entire cohort."** No source, study, or first-party data
is attached to this claim.

Sustainability proof points named in the plan are limited to the phrases
"eco-friendly," "planet-first," and "less plastic." There is no lifecycle
assessment, no third-party certification, no ingredient disclosure, and no stated
figure for how much plastic a customer actually avoids by switching.

## Channels and channel roles

Paid media is concentrated on **Instagram** (Feed, Reels, and Stories), which the
plan describes as "where Millennials are." The stated roles:

- **Instagram** — awareness, consideration, and conversion (all three).
- **YouTube** — a small bumper-ad awareness test.
- **Email** — "we will send some emails to buyers."
- **Search** — not included in this plan.

Channel roles are asserted rather than justified. There is no mapping of each
channel to a specific customer state, decision, or measured behavior, and no
rationale for excluding search despite the category having clear high-intent
queries ("refillable cleaning spray," "plastic-free all-purpose cleaner").

## Creator strategy

Partner with **12 macro-influencers** (500,000 to 2,000,000 followers each) for
one paid post each. Selection criterion, as written: **"largest reach per
dollar."** The brief does not mention category credibility, whether the creator
actually uses refillable products, ongoing relationship, audience-fit, or how FTC
disclosure will be handled. Success for the creator activation is defined as
total follower reach delivered.

## Budget allocation

Total paid media budget: **$900,000** over six months.

| Line item | Share | Amount |
|---|---:|---:|
| Instagram (Feed / Reels / Stories) | 70% | $630,000 |
| Creator partnerships | 18% | $162,000 |
| YouTube bumper awareness test | 7% | $63,000 |
| Email platform and tooling | 3% | $27,000 |
| Contingency | 2% | $18,000 |

The allocation is itemized and internally adds up, but the mix leans heavily on
one platform.

## Conversion event

The defined conversion event is a **first purchase of a Rootwell Starter Kit at
rootwell-example.com**, tracked as a single purchase event in analytics.

## Measurement and KPIs

- **Primary success metric: total impressions.** The plan sets a headline target
  of **120,000,000 impressions** across paid and creator placements and reports
  progress against that number.
- Secondary metric: engagement rate on Instagram and creator posts.
- The Starter-Kit purchase event is tracked, but revenue and CAC appear only in
  the business-objective section, not in the measurement plan's success criteria.
- There is **no holdout, geo-test, or incrementality design**. The plan assumes
  that impressions lead to sales.
- There is **no measurement of repeat purchase, Refill Club retention, or
  customer lifetime value**, even though the business model depends on customers
  buying refills after the first kit.

## The onboarding and refill-reminder email flow

The plan includes a fully specified **post-purchase onboarding and
refill-reminder email sequence** for new Starter-Kit buyers:

1. A welcome email that shows, step by step, how to mix a pod with tap water and
   how to store the bottle.
2. A "you're about halfway through your pods" reminder, timed to the customer's
   purchase date, with a transparent per-use cost comparison (cost per bottle of
   cleaner when refilling versus repurchasing a conventional spray bottle) and a
   one-tap reorder link.
3. A gentle Refill Club invitation that explains cancel-anytime terms in plain
   language before asking for the subscription.

The email flow is written in plain, non-preachy language, includes alt text on
images, uses high-contrast type, and states shipping and cancellation terms
up front. It is the most operationally concrete and customer-useful part of the
plan. It is funded only through the 3% email-tooling line and its outcomes are
not part of the success metrics above.

## Constraints

- Launch creative must be in market within four weeks.
- US regulatory context applies, including FTC endorsement-disclosure
  expectations for paid creators and standard email-consent practice.
- Brand voice guideline: warm, plain-spoken, and non-preachy.
- Brand accessibility standard requires captions on video and alt text on images,
  though the plan does not describe applying this standard to social or creator
  content.
- Margin note: the $28 CAC ceiling is higher than the $24 first-order price, so
  first orders are acquired at roughly break-even or a slight loss; profitability
  depends on refill and subscription behavior after the first purchase.

---

## Your task

Review this media plan for its intended audience and tell the team whether it is
likely to work, why, what is weak or unsupported, and what should change or be
tested.

# Generational Marketing Review

## Purpose

Review a marketing plan, campaign, customer experience, or marketing asset for fit with a user-specified generational audience.

Produce a practical answer to:

> Is this likely to work for the specified audience, why, what is weak or unsupported, and what should change or be tested?

Use generation as one audience lens. Do not treat a cohort label as a complete persona or as proof of behavior.

## Use this skill when the user asks to

- review a marketing plan for Gen Z, Zillennials, Millennials, Xennials, Gen X, or another age-defined cohort;
- assess whether creative, copy, offers, channels, or customer experience fit a generation;
- compare one campaign across generations;
- adapt an asset for a different generation;
- identify stereotypes, dated assumptions, or unsupported audience claims;
- create a generation-fit scorecard and test plan.

## Required context

Use the information supplied by the user. Before issuing a definitive verdict, identify whether the following are known:

- target cohort and birth-year or life-stage definition;
- geography and language;
- product or service category;
- customer state or journey stage;
- campaign objective;
- channel and placement;
- asset format;
- offer, price, delivery, returns, and fulfillment constraints;
- brand voice and accessibility requirements;
- source of audience claims;
- success metric.

Do not invent missing information. When context is incomplete, make the smallest reasonable assumption, label it, and reduce confidence.

## Choose a workflow

### Quick scan

Use when the user wants a fast opinion.

Read:

- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Return:

- verdict;
- three strengths;
- three risks;
- three priority changes;
- confidence and missing evidence.

### Full marketing-plan review

Use for campaign plans, briefs, channel plans, launch plans, or lifecycle plans.

Read:

- `references/plan-review.md`
- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/generation-lenses.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Use:

- `assets/review-report-template.md`
- `assets/evidence-register-template.md`

### Marketing-asset review

Use for copy, email, landing pages, product pages, images, video, creator briefs, ads, SMS, push, direct mail, or social posts.

Read:

- `references/asset-review.md`
- `references/review-rubric.md`
- `references/generation-lenses.md`
- `references/evidence-and-safety.md`

Use:

- `assets/review-report-template.md`

### Cross-generation comparison

Review the same plan or asset separately through each requested lens. Then identify:

- shared strengths;
- shared weaknesses;
- conflicting needs;
- what can remain common;
- what should be adapted;
- what requires testing rather than assumption.

## Governing principles

1. **Generation is a lens, not a verdict.**
2. **Behavior, customer state, category, geography, and context can matter more than age.**
3. **Separate fact, observation, inference, assumption, recommendation, and unknown.**
4. **Do not present uncited percentages, platform rankings, posting times, or birth ranges as current facts.**
5. **Do not repeat stereotypes merely because they appeared in source material.**
6. **Translate broad claims into testable hypotheses.**
7. **Do not recommend deceptive, discriminatory, inaccessible, privacy-invasive, or noncompliant marketing.**
8. **A serious legal, privacy, accessibility, trust, or evidence problem can override a high average score.**
9. **Preserve “insufficient evidence” as a valid outcome.**
10. **Prefer specific revisions and experiments over vague advice.**

## Review method

1. Identify the requested audience definition.
2. Identify the objective, customer state, channel, format, and conversion action.
3. Extract every explicit audience claim.
4. Classify each claim as provided fact, observation, inference, assumption, recommendation, or unknown.
5. Review the plan or asset against the rubric.
6. Apply the relevant generation lens as a hypothesis set, not a stereotype set.
7. Identify critical risks and contradictions.
8. Prioritize changes by impact and effort.
9. Propose measurable tests.
10. Return a clear verdict and confidence level.

## Output contract

For a full review, include:

1. **Verdict**
   - Strong fit
   - Promising but needs revision
   - Weak fit
   - Insufficient evidence

2. **Confidence**
   - High
   - Medium
   - Low

3. **Audience-definition check**

4. **Scorecard**
   - dimension;
   - score from 0 to 4;
   - evidence;
   - concern;
   - recommended action.

5. **What works**

6. **What may fail**

7. **Stereotype, evidence, and freshness flags**

8. **Priority fixes**
   - critical;
   - high;
   - medium.

9. **Test plan**
   - hypothesis;
   - variant;
   - primary metric;
   - guardrail;
   - decision rule.

10. **Final recommendation**
    - proceed;
    - revise and retest;
    - gather more evidence;
    - do not proceed.

## Scoring

Use the 0–4 scale defined in `references/review-rubric.md`.

Do not convert the total into a precise probability of success. Use the scorecard to structure judgment, not to create false certainty.

## Public-safe behavior

Do not expose private source material, internal company names, personal data, third-party screenshots, or confidential metrics. Do not copy source language when an independent, neutral formulation is possible.

# Marketing-Plan Review

## 1. Parse the plan

Extract:

- business objective;
- customer objective;
- audience definition;
- customer state;
- proposition;
- offer;
- channel roles;
- content formats;
- journey;
- budget or constraints;
- measurement;
- evidence.

## 2. Find contradictions

Examples:

- broad awareness objective with only conversion creative;
- trust-sensitive product with weak proof;
- social-discovery strategy with a difficult mobile checkout;
- purpose positioning without substantiation;
- creator strategy based only on reach;
- promotion strategy without margin or loyalty guardrails.

## 3. Apply the rubric

Score every dimension and identify critical overrides.

## 4. Apply the audience lens

Use `generation-lenses.md` as questions to ask. Do not give points merely because the plan mentions a platform, trend, creator, coupon, or nostalgic reference.

## 5. Create the change plan

Prioritize changes by:

- customer impact;
- business impact;
- evidence gap;
- execution effort;
- reversibility;
- risk.

## 6. Create the test plan

Every important generational assumption should become one of:

- verified fact;
- first-party analysis;
- qualitative research question;
- experiment;
- unresolved uncertainty.

===== FILE: references/review-rubric.md =====
# Review Rubric

Score every dimension from 0 to 4.

| Score | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Missing, harmful, or directly contradictory |
| 1 | Weak and mostly unsupported |
| 2 | Mixed or incomplete |
| 3 | Strong with minor gaps |
| 4 | Strong, evidenced, and execution-ready |

## Dimensions

### 1. Audience definition

Check whether the cohort, birth range or life stage, geography, category, and customer state are clear.

### 2. Customer need and context

Check whether the plan solves a real need in the correct moment rather than relying on age alone.

### 3. Value proposition

Check clarity, relevance, differentiation, credibility, and expected customer benefit.

### 4. Message and tone

Check language, cultural relevance, respect, readability, and brand fit.

### 5. Creative and format

Check visual hierarchy, pacing, platform-native execution, information density, and production quality.

### 6. Channel and platform fit

Check whether the channel role is justified by evidence, objective, and customer behavior.

### 7. Trust and proof

Check reviews, demonstrations, comparisons, substantiation, transparency, policies, creator credibility, and social proof.

### 8. Offer and purchase friction

Check price communication, discounts, bundles, checkout, payment, and conversion friction.

### 9. Customer experience and fulfillment

Check delivery, returns, support, onboarding, loyalty, and post-purchase expectations.

### 10. Inclusion, accessibility, privacy, and ethics

Check representation, contrast, captions, readability, consent, data use, discriminatory targeting, and manipulative practices.

### 11. Measurement and experimentation

Check objective, primary metric, guardrails, baseline, test design, sample, and decision rule.

### 12. Evidence quality

Check source, recency, geography, methodology, first-party relevance, and whether assumptions are labeled.

## Critical override

A serious problem in accessibility, privacy, legality, deception, discrimination, trust, or evidence can override the average score.

# Generation Lenses

These are hypothesis sets derived from recurring themes in the source material. They are not universal truths. Apply them only after considering category, geography, life stage, customer state, and first-party evidence.

Birth-year ranges vary across sources. Use the user's definition when provided.

## Gen Z

Questions to test:

- Is the creative native to the selected social or video environment?
- Does the content earn attention through usefulness, entertainment, identity, or participation?
- Are creators credible users rather than one-time endorsers?
- Is product discovery connected to clear proof and an easy mobile path to action?
- Are video, community, gaming, trends, or social participation relevant to the category?
- Does the brand avoid condescension, forced slang, and “always online” stereotypes?

Common risks:

- equating the audience with TikTok;
- using a trend without brand relevance;
- overproduced or deceptive creator content;
- weak product proof;
- inaccessible video;
- assuming low attention rather than improving clarity.

## Zillennials

Questions to test:

- Does the plan reflect a hybrid experience of older social platforms and newer mobile-first behavior?
- Can the campaign use cultural memory or nostalgia without becoming exclusionary?
- Does it balance entertainment with adult-level product clarity?
- Are platform, creator, and shopping assumptions validated rather than borrowed from Gen Z or Millennials?

Common risks:

- treating the cohort as a fixed demographic;
- forcing micro-generation references;
- using nostalgia as the value proposition rather than a creative device.

## Millennials

Questions to test:

- Does the brand demonstrate transparency, responsiveness, and useful community participation?
- Are sustainability, inclusion, and purpose claims specific and substantiated?
- Are creators or artists part of a credible, ongoing relationship?
- Does the content respect the audience rather than chasing trends performatively?
- Is the experience visual, convenient, and informative?

Common risks:

- purpose washing;
- performative social stances;
- assuming every customer prioritizes the same values;
- using “authenticity” as a style without operational proof.

## Xennials

Questions to test:

- Does the plan support cross-device research and decision making?
- Are reviews, product demonstrations, comparisons, specifications, returns, and refunds clear?
- Is checkout simple and trustworthy?
- Can nostalgia improve recall without replacing product relevance?
- Are live content, webinars, or longer demonstrations useful in this category?
- Are creators credible long-term users?

Common risks:

- unsupported nostalgia;
- overcomplicated payment or checkout;
- burying essential product details;
- using age-coded creative instead of customer insight.

## Gen X

Questions to test:

- Does the plan provide practical value, clear proof, and a trustworthy purchase experience?
- Are reviews, comparisons, product demonstrations, delivery, returns, and support visible?
- Are promotions or loyalty benefits clear without assuming price is the only motivator?
- Are established channels such as email, search, YouTube, and major social platforms used for a defined role?
- Does the plan support both concise scanning and deeper research?
- Does the creative avoid “forgotten generation,” technology-resistant, or coupon-only stereotypes?

Common risks:

- assuming the cohort only uses Facebook;
- overusing discounts;
- using old-age or nostalgia clichés;
- weak mobile experience;
- long copy without hierarchy;
- treating fast delivery as a universal requirement.

## Cross-generation rule

When evidence is weak, convert the lens into a testable hypothesis rather than a recommendation.

===== FILE: references/evidence-and-safety.md =====
# Evidence and Safety

## Claim labels

Use these exact labels when useful:

- **Provided fact:** Explicitly supplied by the user.
- **Observed feature:** Directly visible in the plan or asset.
- **Inference:** Reasoned from supplied material.
- **Assumption:** Necessary but unverified.
- **Recommendation:** Proposed action.
- **Unknown:** Required information is missing.

## Evidence checks

For a quantitative or behavioral claim, look for:

- source;
- publication date;
- fieldwork date;
- geography;
- sample;
- methodology;
- category relevance;
- first-party confirmation.

Without these, do not present the claim as current fact.

## Prohibited behavior

Do not:

- recommend excluding or disadvantaging protected groups;
- infer sensitive traits from age or creative appearance;
- use dark patterns or deceptive urgency;
- advise evading platform disclosures;
- recommend collecting unnecessary personal data;
- present stereotypes as evidence;
- redistribute copyrighted source assets;
- expose private or confidential inputs.

## Safer transformation

Convert broad demographic claims into:

- a question;
- a hypothesis;
- a test;
- a segment definition;
- a research need;
- a confidence statement.

<review>
## Verdict

As written, this plan is likely to **hit its vanity metric and miss its business objective.** It is optimized to buy 120M impressions, but the money is supposed to buy 40,000 customers at ≤$28 CAC and $2.0M in revenue — and almost nothing in the channel mix, metric set, or budget is actually pointed at those outcomes. The single most valuable asset in the document (the refill email flow) is buried at 3% funding and excluded from the scorecard, even though the unit economics literally can't work without it.

The good news: the fixes are mostly reallocation and reframing, not a teardown.

## The core disconnect (fix this first)

**The success metric measures the wrong thing.** Primary KPI is total impressions; revenue, customers, and CAC live in a different section and aren't tracked as success criteria. There is no holdout or incrementality design, so the plan can't even tell whether impressions *caused* sales. You will be able to report "we delivered 120M impressions" while having no defensible read on whether the $900k worked. Swap the headline: **primary = first-time customers and blended CAC; secondary = revenue, refill attach rate, subscription-start rate, retention.** Impressions become a diagnostic, not the goal.

**The revenue target secretly depends on refills — which nobody is measuring.** Do the arithmetic: 40,000 first-time customers × $24 Starter Kit = **$960k**, less than half the $2.0M goal. To reach $2.0M each customer must generate ~$50 within six months — roughly a kit *plus* two refill packs or a subscription. So the revenue objective is mathematically a **refill-and-retention objective**, yet repeat purchase, Refill Club retention, and LTV are explicitly not measured, and the email flow that drives them is funded only as "tooling." The margin note already admits first orders are break-even-to-loss; profit is 100% downstream of behavior the plan neither funds nor tracks.

**The CAC target is fragile given the mix.** $900k / 40k = $22.50 per customer if *every* dollar and *every* customer converted perfectly — technically under $28, with almost no cushion. But 70% is on awareness-style Instagram plus macro-influencer reach for a **zero-awareness brand asking for an unfamiliar behavior.** That mix does not realistically convert at $22.50 blended. The break-even-or-loss first order plus a thin CAC cushion plus an awareness-heavy plan is how you overspend to CAC and still miss volume.

## Message and audience: the load-bearing assumption is unsupported

The whole creative rests on **"Millennials prioritize sustainability above price and convenience"** — with no source, no first-party data, and, notably, **contradicted by the plan's own customer-state section**, which says most of these people currently buy conventional single-use bottles. Revealed behavior says price and convenience are winning today. Treating ~65M people born across 15 years as one audience with one motivation compounds the risk.

Separately, the sustainability story is **claimed, not proven**: "eco-friendly," "planet-first," "less plastic," with no lifecycle data, no certification, no ingredient disclosure, and no figure for plastic actually avoided. Against a mildly skeptical audience that's weak persuasion, and under FTC Green Guides, vague green claims are a compliance exposure, not just a soft sell.

The real barrier isn't awareness of sustainability — it's **friction and uncertainty about the refill behavior** ("do I really drop a pod in tap water and trust it works?"). A feel-good awareness message doesn't reduce that friction. The provable, behavior-relevant benefits — cost-per-bottle savings, convenience, less clutter, "one kit replaces X bottles a year" — are stronger hooks, and they're exactly what the (excellent) email flow already leans on. Sustainability should be a supporting reason-to-believe, not the sole bet resting on an unproven premise.

## Channel and creator problems

- **Instagram doing all three funnel jobs at 70%** is single-platform concentration risk, and one awareness-native surface rarely does awareness *and* efficient conversion well.
- **No search** is the clearest miss. The plan concedes there are high-intent queries ("refillable cleaning spray," "plastic-free all-purpose cleaner"). That's cheap, ready-to-convert demand — the fastest path to a defensible CAC — and it's excluded while break-even first orders are being bought elsewhere. Add branded + high-intent non-brand search.
- **Creator strategy is optimized for reach, not trust or conversion.** 12 macro creators, one post each, chosen on "largest reach per dollar," success = follower reach. For a trust-and-behavior-change product you want *demonstration* and credibility: fewer macro, more mid/micro creators who genuinely use refillables, multi-touch or how-to content, and success measured on conversions/assisted conversions, not raw reach. And the brief omits **FTC #ad disclosure entirely**, which is a stated regulatory constraint — that's a compliance gap, not an oversight to fix later.
- **Accessibility standard isn't applied to social/creator/YouTube.** The brand requires captions on video and alt text on images; the plan only applies this to email. Captions on Reels/bumpers are both compliance *and* reach (sound-off viewing).

## What's genuinely good (keep and elevate)

- **The onboarding/refill email flow is the best thing in the plan** — concrete, on-brand (plain, non-preachy), accessible (alt text, high contrast), transparent on cost and cancellation. It's also the exact mechanism that drives the refills the revenue math requires. It should be a **funded, measured growth pillar with its own targets** (open→reorder rate, Refill Club start rate, 90/180-day retention), not a 3% tooling line.
- Budget is itemized, adds up, and includes a contingency line.
- The conversion event is clearly defined, and the margin note is honest about break-even.

## What to change or test

1. **Reframe KPIs** to customers, CAC, revenue, refill attach, subscription-start, and retention. Demote impressions to diagnostic.
2. **Fund and measure retention.** Move email/CRM out of "tooling" into a real line with targets; the profit engine lives here.
3. **Add search** (branded + high-intent generic) to capture existing demand and lower blended CAC.
4. **Rebalance off 70% single-platform** toward conversion + retention; give Instagram a defined funnel role rather than all three.
5. **Rebuild the creator brief:** category credibility and demonstration over raw reach, mandatory FTC disclosure, conversion-based success.
6. **A/B the message assumption** instead of asserting it: sustainability-led vs. value/convenience-led vs. combined. Let the data decide; revealed behavior suggests value may win.
7. **Substantiate or soften green claims** — quantify plastic avoided, add ingredient transparency or a cert (Green Guides risk otherwise).
8. **Add a lightweight incrementality read** — a geo holdout or matched-market test is cheap insurance on a $900k launch.
9. **Apply the accessibility standard everywhere** (captions on Reels/bumpers, alt text on social).
10. **Sanity-check feasibility in-model:** with 40k customers needing ~$50 each to reach $2.0M, either the customer target, the AOV/refill assumption, or the revenue target needs to be reconciled before launch.

The four-week timeline is achievable, but not for 12 vetted, disclosure-compliant macro partnerships plus new creative — so use the reframe to start narrower (search + a demonstration-led creator test + the email flow) and scale the winners.

# Generational Marketing Review

## Verdict

**Fit:** Weak fit (as written)
**Confidence:** Medium
**Recommended decision:** Revise and retest

## Audience-definition check

- **Cohort:** US Millennials (single, undifferentiated audience).
- **Birth range or life stage:** 1981–1996, ~ages 29–44 (*Provided fact*, plan's own definition — used as given). Note: this span covers very different household states — early-career renters through mid-career homeowners and parents — which matters a great deal for a household-cleaning purchase and a refill-adoption behavior.
- **Geography:** United States only (*Provided fact*).
- **Category:** Household cleaning; DTC refillable/concentrate system (*Provided fact*).
- **Customer state:** Near-zero brand awareness, moderate category awareness, mostly current single-use buyers; must be convinced both to try a new brand and to adopt an unfamiliar refill behavior (*Provided fact*).
- **Objective:** $2.0M net new DTC revenue, 40,000 first-time customers, CAC ≤ $28, six-month H2 window (*Provided fact*).
- **Missing context:** Any intra-cohort segmentation (household composition, homeownership, income, region, prior eco/refill purchase behavior); the source behind the sustainability-priority claim; whether the product carries any real substantiation (LCA, certification, ingredient disclosure, quantified plastic avoided); checkout, returns, and support details; first-party audience data; and whether the brand's own accessibility standard will be applied to social and creator video.

## Executive summary

The plan has a clear commercial objective and one genuinely strong, execution-ready asset: the post-purchase onboarding and refill-reminder email flow. That flow is the only part of the plan that addresses the actual hard problem — getting a first-time buyer to adopt a new behavior and keep refilling — and it is accessible, transparent, and non-preachy.

Everything around it undercuts the objective. The strategy rests on an unsourced, monolithic assumption ("Millennials prioritize sustainability above price and convenience across the entire cohort") that is treated as fact and drives channel, message, and creative choices. The sustainability positioning has no substantiation, which is both a trust weakness and a legal exposure. The primary success metric is total impressions on a business whose objective is revenue, customers, and CAC — and whose economics only work *after* the first order, because acquisition is break-even-to-loss at a $28 CAC on a $24 kit. Yet there is no measurement of refills, retention, or LTV, no incrementality design, undisclosed reach-only creators, and no search despite obvious high-intent demand. As written, this plan is unlikely to hit $2.0M profitably and carries compliance risk. It is salvageable, but the fixes are structural, not cosmetic.

## Scorecard

| Dimension | Score 0–4 | Evidence | Concern | Recommended action |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Audience definition | 2 | Cohort, birth range, geography, category, and customer state are all clearly stated. | Treated as one undifferentiated block; no segmentation despite wide life-stage spread and a behavior-change goal. | Define 2–3 actionable segments (e.g., current eco/refill triers vs. price/convenience-first switchers) and test messaging per segment. |

## What works

- **The onboarding and refill-reminder email flow** (*Observed feature*): step-by-step behavior instruction, transparent per-use cost comparison, one-tap reorder, plain-language cancel-anytime terms, alt text, and high-contrast type. This is the strongest, most customer-useful, and most compliant element and it directly targets the plan's hardest problem — behavior adoption and repeat purchase.
- **A specific, honest offer**: clear prices and cancel-anytime terms, consistent with the Millennial preference for transparency.
- **A defined commercial objective** with an explicit CAC ceiling, which makes the plan testable and gives clear success criteria to align the rest of the strategy to.
- **A well-articulated customer state** that correctly names the dual barrier (new brand + new behavior), even if the media strategy does not act on it.

## What may fail

- **The strategy inherits its own foundational assumption.** Positioning, channel choice, and creative all flow from an unsourced claim that the whole cohort ranks sustainability above price and convenience. If that is wrong for even a large minority, the primary message misses the switchers who currently buy on price/convenience.
- **Vanity primary metric.** Optimizing to 120M impressions can be "achieved" while revenue, CAC, and customer targets are missed; impressions are not evidence of incremental sales.
- **Broken unit economics with no retention plan.** First orders are acquired at roughly break-even or a loss; profitability depends entirely on refills and subscription — which nothing in the media plan drives or measures except the underfunded email flow.
- **Single-platform concentration + excluded search.** 70% on Instagram plus reach-only creators leaves high-intent demand ("refillable cleaning spray," "plastic-free all-purpose cleaner") uncaptured and creates fragility if IG performance is soft.
- **Greenwashing exposure.** Vague eco claims with no substantiation can fail FTC Green Guides expectations and erode the exact trust Millennials weight heavily.
- **Undisclosed, non-credible creators.** Reach-only macro one-shots with no stated FTC disclosure and no evidence of actually using the product risk both weak performance and a compliance problem.
- **Accessibility gap in social/creator video.** The brand's own captions/alt-text standard is not applied where most of the budget runs.

## Stereotype, evidence, and freshness flags

- **Stereotype presented as fact:** "Millennials prioritize sustainability above price and convenience... across the entire cohort." This is an *Assumption*, not a *Provided fact*. It ignores category, life stage, household economics, and prior behavior, and treats a cohort label as a complete persona. Do not scale spend on it unverified.
- **Stereotype / unjustified channel claim:** "Instagram is where Millennials are." An *Assumption* used to justify 70% of budget and three funnel roles. Platform rankings for an audience are not a stable, uncited fact — validate against first-party and channel behavior for this category.
- **Purpose-washing risk:** "Eco-friendly," "planet-first," and "less plastic" are unsubstantiated. Millennial-facing sustainability claims require specific, verifiable proof; the plan supplies none.
- **Freshness/economics contradiction:** The measurement section measures the wrong thing (impressions) for the objective (revenue/CAC), and omits the retention metrics the business model requires.
- **No uncited statistics introduced:** No percentages, posting times, or platform rankings are asserted here as current fact; the plan's single quantitative behavioral claim is flagged as an untested assumption.

## Priority fixes

### Critical

1. **Substantiate or remove the environmental claims.** Before launch, back "sustainable" with specific proof (quantified plastic avoided per switch, ingredient disclosure, and/or third-party certification) or stop making the claim. This is a legal (FTC Green Guides) and trust issue that overrides average score.
2. **Replace the primary success metric.** Make CAC, first purchases, and blended contribution the success criteria; demote impressions to a diagnostic. A revenue/CAC objective cannot be steered by an impressions target.
3. **Instrument and fund the retention engine.** Add refill repeat rate, Refill Club activation, and per-customer contribution as first-class KPIs, and resource the email flow accordingly — the model is unprofitable without them given break-even acquisition.
4. **Enforce FTC disclosure and apply the accessibility standard everywhere.** Require conspicuous paid-partnership disclosure on every creator post and captions/alt text on all social and creator video, not just email.

### High

5. **Add non-brand search** for high-intent category queries and give each channel a single, evidence-based role tied to a customer state; reduce single-platform concentration.
6. **Rebuild the creator brief** around category credibility, genuine product use, demonstration of the mixing behavior, and ongoing relationships; change the success definition from reach to first purchases within CAC.
7. **Move a provable, tangible benefit into the headline proposition** (cost-per-use and quantified plastic avoided), rather than reserving it for the email flow.

### Medium

8. **Segment the audience** into at least a value/convenience-first switcher segment and an eco-motivated segment; message and measure separately.
9. **Add an acquisition-time path to Refill Club** (bundle or incentive) and document a low-friction mobile checkout.
10. **Align creative copy with the "non-preachy" brand voice** and specify returns/support alongside onboarding.

## Test plan

| Hypothesis | Variant | Primary metric | Guardrail | Decision rule |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sustainability-first messaging does **not** universally beat value/convenience-forward messaging for this cohort in this category. | A: sustainability-first creative; B: benefit-forward ("saves money per bottle + less hassle + less plastic"). | Cost per first purchase (CPA). | No unsubstantiated green claims in either arm; equal spend and audience. | Scale the arm with lower CPA at/under $28; if B ≥ A, retire the "whole-cohort sustainability" assumption. |
| High-intent search captures ready-to-switch buyers at lower CAC than Instagram conversion. | Add a non-brand search campaign for category queries alongside IG. | CAC by channel. | Capped test budget; exclude brand terms to isolate incremental intent. | If search CAC ≤ IG conversion CAC, reallocate budget toward search. |
| Paid impressions are actually driving incremental sales. | Geo holdout: matched markets on vs. off. | Incremental revenue / iROAS. | Pre-set minimum detectable effect and test duration. | Scale only channels/markets showing positive incrementality; cut those that don't. |
| The onboarding + refill email flow lifts refill and subscription behavior enough to make break-even acquisition profitable. | A: full flow; B: receipt-only control. | 90-day refill repeat rate + Refill Club activation + 6-month contribution per customer. | Unsubscribe/spam-complaint rate below threshold. | If A raises contribution above CAC by target margin, fully fund and expand the flow. |
| Category-credible creators with a demo beat reach-only macro one-shots on cost-efficient conversion. | A: mid-tier credible product users with mixing demo; B: macro reach buys. | First purchases per creator dollar (CPA). | 100% FTC disclosure compliance; captions on all video. | Shift creator budget to whichever drives purchases within CAC; drop reach-only if it underperforms. |
| Quantified, substantiated proof converts better than vague eco language. | A: PDP/creative with quantified proof (plastic avoided, cost-per-use, certification); B: vague "eco-friendly." | Landing-to-purchase conversion rate. | All claims substantiated per FTC Green Guides before running. | Adopt the higher-CVR proven variant; do not scale any unsubstantiated claim. |

## Final recommendation

**Revise and retest.** Do not launch the current strategy as the plan to hit $2.0M. Keep the objective and the email flow, which are the real assets. Before or at launch, resolve the four critical items — substantiate or drop the green claims, change the primary success metric to CAC/purchases/contribution, instrument and fund the retention engine, and enforce FTC disclosure plus accessibility across all placements. Then run the message, search, incrementality, retention, creator, and proof tests above, and reallocate budget by measured CAC and contribution rather than by the assumption that Millennials and Instagram are interchangeable with the objective. Reassess for a fuller "go" once the sustainability-priority hypothesis is validated with first-party evidence and the refill economics are shown to clear the break-even acquisition cost.
